Introduction

[
1
]

The defendants, Craig E. Jones, Q.C., Timothy C.
Louman-Gardiner, John I. McLean, Q.C., and Colin Brousson (the “Lawyer
defendants”); the defendants, Hong Guo and Guo Law Corporation (the “Guo
defendants”); and the defendant Craig A. Munro apply pursuant to Rule 9-5 of
the
Supreme Court Civil Rules,
B.C. Reg. 168/2009 [
Rules
], to
have the notice of civil claim struck as disclosing no reasonable cause of
action; as being unnecessary, frivolous or vexatious; and as being an abuse of
process. In addition, the Lawyer defendants apply pursuant to Rule 9-6(5)(a)  to
have the action dismissed as not raising a genuine issue for trial. The
defendant Bryant Mackey appeared at the hearing acting on his own behalf. Mr. Mackey
adopted the submissions made by counsel for the Lawyer defendants and Mr.
Munro’s counsel seeking to strike the notice of civil claim.

[
2
]

The Lawyer defendants further seek an order
declaring Mr. Grosz a vexatious litigant pursuant to
s. 18
of the
Supreme
Court Act
, R.S.B.C. 1996, c. 443, and that he be precluded from commencing
any further actions without leave of the court, and other restrictive orders.
This application was supported by all of the other defendants.

[
3
]

Mr. Grosz represented himself in this action, as
he has in all of the actions he has brought to date.

[
4
]

I will first deal with the issues relating to
the setting of the application and the request for an adjournment made by Mr.
Grosz at the commencement of the hearing.

Procedural Background

[
5
]

The notice of civil claim was filed on November
12, 2019, after Mr. Grosz obtained an order for indigent status to waive the filing
fees. On the day that Mr. Grosz filed the notice of civil claim in this
action, he sent in a Request to Appear seeking, among other things, a hearing
date for the consolidation of this action with the
Grosz v. Guo
, Van.
Reg. S178289, action (the “First Guo Action”). This was followed the next day
with another Request to Appear seeking an appearance before me in this action
and five other actions. As part of this request, he sought leave to apply to
disqualify the following counsel: Paul Arvisais, Nicholas Safarik, Colin
Brousson, and Timothy Louman-Gardiner, as being “conflicted” in two other
actions, being Van. Reg. B170021 and Van. Reg. S199755.

[
6
]

On November 26, 2019, the Lawyer defendants
filed a response to civil claim. On November 29, 2019, the Guo defendants and
Mr. Mackey filed responses to civil claim. On December 4, 2019, Mr. Munro filed
a response to civil claim. All of the responses allege that all or part of the
claim is “frivolous, vexatious, and an abuse of the process of this Honourable
Court”.

[
7
]

On December 19, 2019, the case was assigned to
me by the Chief Justice to case manage. At that time, I had already seized
myself of or been assigned the following cases involving Mr. Grosz to case
manage:

a.

Van. Reg. B170021 – In the Matter of the Bankruptcy of Guo Law
Corporation (the “Insolvency Proceeding”);

b.

Van. Reg. S178289 – the First Guo Action;

c.

Van. Reg. S145050 – Matryx Corporation v. Royal Trust Corporation
(the “First Royal Trust Action”); and

d.

Van. Reg. S199755 – Grosz v. Royal Trust Corporation (the “Second
Royal Trust Action”).

[
8
]

On December 19, 2019, counsel for the Lawyer
defendants sent in a Request to Appear for dates in February for an application
to strike and an application to have the plaintiff declared a vexatious
litigant.

[
9
]

By January 23, 2020, the dates of February 26 to
28, 2020 were provided to hear the defendants’ applications to strike and to
have Mr. Grosz declared a vexatious litigant.

[
10
]

The applications of the various defendants were
filed on:

a.

February 12, 2020 – application of the Guo defendants seeking to
strike;

b.

February 13, 2020 – application of Mr. Munro seeking to strike; and

c.

February 13, 2020 – application of the Lawyer defendants seeking to
strike and a vexatious litigant order.

[
11
]

Mr. Grosz did not file any application responses
as required by the
Rules
.

[
12
]

The date of February 25, 2020, had been reserved
for Mr. Grosz to bring a recusal application. He filed the application seeking
to have me recuse myself on February 24, 2020 in
Minoru Stakeholders Society
v. Minoru View Homes Ltd
., Van. Reg. S200020 (the “Minoru Action”), another
action brought by Mr. Grosz that I was assigned to case manage. He was not able
to properly serve the defendants with the application materials in accordance
with the
Rules
. At the hearing on February 25, 2020, Mr. Grosz was given
an option of proceeding with the recusal application on the materials he had
filed (the defendants agreed to this), or having his recusal application
adjourned so as to give him more time to prepare materials. Mr. Grosz indicated
his preference for an adjournment, and one was granted. It was made clear to
him that the applications in this action scheduled for February 26 to 28, 2020
would proceed.

[
13
]

The recusal application was set down for May 19,
2020, with deadlines. This application was not heard since Mr. Grosz sought an
adjournment due to issues relating to the COVID-19 crisis.

[
14
]

On the morning of February 26, 2020, Mr. Grosz
handed up a binder titled “Jurisdictional Response” and his affidavit #3. These
documents had not been previously served on the defendants. Mr. Grosz took the
position that, since he was planning to start a claim in the Federal Court that
involved many of the same defendants in this action and some of the same
claims, the Supreme Court of British Columbia and Court of Appeal for British
Columbia had lost jurisdiction and could not hear these applications. He sought
an adjournment to allow him time to prepare his jurisdictional submissions.

[
15
]

The defendants opposed an adjournment of the
applications. I agreed to hear the merits of the defendants’ submissions and
then consider the jurisdictional response and authorities that Mr. Grosz cited.
I did so and I have addressed the merits of Mr. Grosz’s jurisdictional argument
in my reasons indexed at
Grosz v. Guo
,
2020 BCSC 997
at paras.
9–18
(the
“Injunction Reasons”), which dealt with another application for which Mr. Grosz
raised the same argument. I found there was no merit in his position since the
proposed Federal Court claim involves different parties and different
underlying conduct; the action before me did not involve any relief claimed
against the Crown and none of the other provisions of the
Federal Courts Act
,
R.S.C. 1985, c. F-7, conferring jurisdiction on the Federal Court appeared to
apply; and the doctrine of paramountcy did not apply to give the Federal Court
jurisdiction. All of these reasons apply equally to this application. I am not
satisfied that this Court has been deprived of its jurisdiction over this
matter.

[
16
]

At the end of the defendants’ submissions, Mr.
Grosz sought an adjournment so he could have time to prepare application
responses and a written argument. In order to accommodate him, I agreed to
this.  He advised me that he was “too busy” to prepare anything until after
March 13
th
. I made the following orders in respect to deadlines:

a.

Mr. Grosz had to file his application responses, limited to 10 pages
each, and any responding affidavits by March 23, 2020 at 4 p.m.;

b.

Mr. Grosz had leave to file a written argument that was no longer
than 70 pages; and

c.

the defendants had until April 3, 2020 at 4 p.m. to file any reply
materials.

[
17
]

I made the following interim order:

Mr. Grosz, in
his own capacity, or as a director or officer of any corporation, or on behalf
of any society, is prohibited from commencing any proceeding in the Supreme
Court of British Columbia without first obtaining leave of this court. This
interim order shall be in effect until reasons have been pronounced on the
applications brought by the defendants in this action on February 26, 2020.

[
18
]

At Mr. Grosz’s request, I extended his March 23,
2020 deadline to May 15, 2020 at 4 p.m. The defendants’ deadline for any reply
materials was extended to June 1, 2020. On May 4, 2020, I provided a memorandum
to address issues that Mr. Grosz had raised respecting filing materials.
My memorandum stated, in part:

Grosz v. Jones (S1912718)

On May 1, 2020, the Alberta Court of Appeal
released reasons in
Jonsson v. Lymer
,
2020 ABCA 167
which dealt with the
scope of a court’s inherent jurisdiction to restrain vexatious litigation, the
proper breadth of vexatious litigant orders, and related procedural issues. The
reasons included some broader discussion of vexatious litigant orders. Some of
the comments would only apply in Alberta but many of the comments have general
application.

Since Mr. Grosz has until May 15, 2020 at 4
p.m., as provided in my memorandum of March 26, 2020, to file and serve his
application responses, any responding materials, and written submissions he can
consider whether he wishes to make reference to this case. The defendants can
also consider whether they wish to comment on this case in their reply
submissions. If Mr. Grosz does not submit any materials by the May 15, 2020
deadline the defendants have leave to provide reply submissions solely related
to this case.

Submissions of materials

In emails that Mr. Grosz sent on April 29,
2020 he raised concerns on how he could file application responses and have
affidavits affirmed or sworn and filed during the current restrictions in the
court’s normal operations. For materials for the pending matters before me, and
during this COVID-19 crisis, Mr. Grosz can provide his materials on the
following basis:

a.

application responses can be signed and then emailed to counsel and
to
sc.civil_va@bccourts.ca
. When
the registry has reopened and Mr. Grosz can personally attend, the signed
application response can be filed by Mr. Grosz and a filed copy of the
application response shall be served on counsel for the parties.

b.

affidavits can be signed by Mr. Grosz and then emailed to counsel
and to
sc.civil_va@bccourts.ca
.
When the registry has reopened and Mr. Grosz can personally attend, he can have
the affidavit properly affirmed or sworn and filed. The affidavit must be an
exact duplicate of what he previously signed and emailed to counsel and the
registry. The properly affirmed or sworn filed affidavit shall be served on
counsel for the parties.

c.

written submissions need only be signed and emailed to counsel and
to
sc.civil_va@bccourts.ca
. There
is no need to file the written submissions.

d.

I am authorizing these procedures to accommodate the requests made
by Mr. Grosz and so there are no further delays in having the materials he
needs to prepare delivered in accordance with the deadlines provided in the
March 26, 2020 memorandum.

[
19
]

Mr. Grosz, again, requested to adjourn all
deadlines. He was given a further deadline of May 19, 2020 at 9 a.m. to provide
materials. He did not do so.

[
20
]

Mr. Munro provided supplemental written
submissions respecting the decision in
Jonsson v. Lymer
,
2020 ABCA 167
,
on June 1, 2020, in compliance with my May 4, 2020 direction.

[
21
]

I turn now to the merits of the applications
before me. I will first provide some background on who the parties are, what
their roles were, and some relevant facts. I will then consider the applications
to strike the action, followed by the vexatious litigant application of the
Lawyer defendants.

Factual Background

[
22
]

Mr. Grosz worked at the law firm of the Guo
defendants from approximately October 2016 to August 2017.  He was employed,
according to Mr. Grosz, as a designated paralegal. Ms. Guo is a lawyer and
principal of the defendant Guo Law Corporation (“GLC”).

[
23
]

The defendant, Craig Elton Jones, first met Mr.
Grosz when he was employed at GLC. Mr. Jones was counsel for Ms. Guo in some
matters.

[
24
]

On January 6, 2017, GLC filed a Notice of
Intention to File a Proposal pursuant to Part III, Division I of the
Bankruptcy
and Insolvency Act
, R.S.C. 1985, c. B-3 [
BIA
], referenced in these
reasons as the Insolvency Proceeding.

[
25
]

On January 6, 2017, G. Powroznik Group Inc. was
appointed as the proposal trustee (the “Initial Proposal Trustee”).

[
26
]

By order of Justice Kent, on January 13, 2017,
in the Insolvency Proceeding, the Initial Proposal Trustee was substituted by
FTI Consulting Canada Inc. (“FTI” or the “Proposal Trustee”), who had consented
to act as the proposal trustee. The defendant, Mr. Munro, is a licensed trustee
in bankruptcy and a managing director of FTI.

[
27
]

On September 5, 2017, Mr. Grosz commenced
proceedings against the Guo defendants in the First Guo Action. The action
sought relief for unpaid wages, alleged sexual harassment, alleged wrongful
dismissal, and punitive damages.

[
28
]

On or about September 5, 2017, Mr. Grosz filed
an amended supplemental proof of claim in the Insolvency Proceeding claiming
unpaid wages of $20,199.04 and $8,249.43, as well as damages totalling $500,000
for the alleged sexual harassment.

[
29
]

The defendant, Timothy Louman-Gardiner, acted as
counsel for GLC in the Insolvency Proceeding up until November 2018. He then
became counsel for GLC again in the fall of 2019. The defendant, Colin
Brousson, is counsel for FTI in the Insolvency Proceeding. Mr. McLean is a partner
of Mr. Brousson who happened to be in chambers on October 2, 2007 when Mr.
Grosz was applying for default judgment against the Guo defendants in the First
Guo Action. Mr. McLean advised the Master hearing the application that his
partner, Mr. Brousson, was counsel for the trustee.

[
30
]

On or about October 4, 2017, Mr. Grosz sought,
with the consent of all parties, the lifting of the stay of proceedings imposed
pursuant to the
BIA
so that he could proceed with the First Guo Action.
On October 18, 2017, the Proposal Trustee consented to the lifting of the stay
and an order was granted to that effect.

[
31
]

The defendant Bryant Mackey provided legal
advice to the Guo defendants respecting the First Guo Action and filed the
response to civil claim. On March 5, 2019, a notice of change of counsel was
filed in the First Guo Action appointing Mr. Louman-Gardiner as counsel
for the defendants.

[
32
]

Both Mr. Jones and Mr. Mackey were involved in
negotiating the settlement of the First Guo Action with Mr. Grosz.

[
33
]

The First Guo Action was settled for the payment
of $5,000 to Mr. Grosz in exchange for a mutual release and a consent dismissal
order. The mutual release was signed on January 18, 2018 and the consent
dismissal order filed March 22, 2018 (the “CDO”).

[
34
]

On February 26, 2019, Mr. Grosz applied to set
aside the CDO. That application was heard on March 4 and 5, 2020 and was
dismissed; see my reasons indexed at
2020 BCSC 1073

(the “CDO Reasons”).

[
35
]

On June 3, 2019, the Guo defendants sought to
have Mr. Grosz declared a vexatious litigant. That application was heard by
Justice Mayer and was unsuccessful; see reasons indexed at
2019 BCSC 1545
(the
“Mayer Reasons”).

Nature of Allegations made

[
36
]

In his notice of civil claim, Mr. Grosz attaches
as Schedule “A” the notice of civil claim in the First Guo Action, and states,
“its entire contents are hereby repleaded and incorporated herein.” The notice
of civil claim is difficult to follow but upon my reading of it, the following
allegations are made:

a.

Mr. Jones filed a false statement to the Richmond RCMP on or about
August 1, 2017, causing Mr. Grosz to be arrested;

b.

On November 1, 2017, Mr. Jones attended in court in Vancouver, and
Mr. Grosz, seeing him there, believed he was going to testify on his
affidavit. This pressured Mr. Grosz into agreeing to a settlement of the First
Guo Action;

c.

Mr. Jones attached confidential documents to an affidavit which
violated solicitor-client privilege;

d.

Ms. Guo reported to the Richmond RCMP false accusations of criminal
harassment, extortion, sexual assault, and uttering threats on or about July 23
and September 1, 2017;

e.

Ms. Guo had her accountant sign and submit a false Record of
Employment and assist her in embezzling $4 million;

f.

Mr. Mackey used his position as a lawyer to
influence law enforcement;

g.

Mr. McLean was in the public gallery on October 2, 2017 when Mr.
Grosz was seeking a default judgment in the First Guo Action and Mr. McLean
interrupted the proceedings from the gallery, making “false submissions” in
order to assist in defeating Mr. Grosz’s application;

h.

Mr. Munro took the position that Mr. Grosz was no longer a creditor
of GLC since a consent dismissal order had been filed in the First Guo Action;
and

i.

“GUO, JONES, MACKEY, LOUMAN, MUNRO, BROUSSON,
and MCLEAN have conspired to damage GROSZ, and that their conspiracy is alive
and well. In the course of their conspiracy each of them slandered, libelled
and defamed GROSZ.”

[
37
]

Mr. Grosz seeks the following relief in this
action:

a.

consolidation of this action with the First Guo Action, as “they are
essentially parallel”;

b.

consolidation of this action with the Insolvency Proceeding and
“other related proceedings”;

c.

all the relief he sought in the First Guo Action;

d.

damages against the Guo defendants resulting from public mischief,
malicious prosecution, extortion, conspiracy to damage and conspiracy by
unlawful means, defamation, and negligence;

e.

damages against Mr. Jones resulting from public mischief, malicious
prosecution, extortion, conspiracy to damage and conspiracy by unlawful means,
defamation, negligence, nonfeasance, misfeasance, and malfeasance;

f.

damages against Mr. Mackey from public mischief,
malicious prosecution, extortion, conspiracy to damage and conspiracy by
unlawful means, defamation, negligence, nonfeasance, misfeasance, and
malfeasance;

g.

damages against Mr. Munro and Mr. Brousson resulting from conspiracy
to damage and conspiracy by unlawful means, defamation, and negligence,
nonfeasance, misfeasance, and malfeasance;

h.

damages against Mr. McLean resulting from conspiracy to damage and
conspiracy by unlawful means, defamation, and negligence; and

i.

as against all of the defendants, damages for
intentional infliction of mental suffering.

[
38
]

Mr. Grosz also seeks to hold each defendant
jointly and severally liable for the torts of the others. Finally, he seeks
“general, special and punitive damages, court order interest, court fees, and
special costs.”

Issue 1: Should the claim against
the Lawyer defendants and Mr. Mackey be dismissed under R. 9-6(5)(a)?

Legal Principles

[
39
]

Rule 9-6(5)(a) provides that the court must
dismiss a claim or pronounce judgment if it is satisfied that it raises no
genuine issue for trial.

[
40
]

Unlike an application under Rule 9-5(1)(a),
which is based on the pleadings alone, an application under Rule 9-6 also
involves the consideration of evidence. The judge should not weigh evidence,
but “may draw inferences that are strongly supported by undisputed facts”:
Kerfoot
v. Richter
,
2018 BCCA 238
at para.
31
. Where there are disputed facts, the
applicant “bears the evidentiary burden of showing that there is no genuine
issue to be tried”:
Kerfoot
at para.
29
.

[
41
]

The question is whether there is a
bona fide

issue to be tried based on the material before the court. If the judge is
required to weigh the evidence to come to a conclusion, then the case is not
appropriate to be decided under this Rule.

Position of the Lawyer defendants

[
42
]

The Lawyer defendants seek an order pursuant to
R. 9-6(5)(a) that the action be dismissed as there is no genuine issue for
trial. In their notice of application, they submit that the notice of civil
claim contains little but speculation and unfounded suspicion. They argue that
Mr. Jones’ affidavit supports that there is simply no basis for any of the
“scurrilous claims” made against him. The material facts in the notice of civil
claim do not even purport to raise a triable issue as against the other
lawyers.

Analysis

[
43
]

I will deal specifically with the allegations
made against each of the lawyers.

[
44
]

The claim against Mr. McLean appears to be
limited to him advising a master in chambers that his law partner was counsel
for the Proposal Trustee. There is no genuine issue that arises from this
action.

[
45
]

The claim being advanced against Mr. Brousson is
not clear in the notice of civil claim. He is alleged to be part of some type
of conspiracy, but there are no particulars of the claim for conspiracy or Mr.
Brousson’s role in it. I am satisfied that there is no genuine issue respecting
Mr. Brousson contained in the notice of civil claim based on the materials before
me.

[
46
]

The claims against Mr. Louman-Gardiner are also
not clear, except the bald statement that he is a party of a conspiracy with
the other defendants. Under Part 2 of the relief sought, Mr. Louman-Gardiner is
not even referenced. The notice of civil claim makes references to times that
this lawyer appeared in court, but this alone is not an actionable act. There
is no genuine issue that has been pled against this lawyer.

[
47
]

All of the claims against Mr. Mackey and Mr.
Jones relating to their role as counsel for the Guo defendants, including the
negotiation of the settlement, are ones that do not raise a genuine issue.
These two lawyers, while acting as counsel for the Guo defendants, owed no duty
to Mr. Grosz.

[
48
]

Mr. Grosz’s allegation that Mr. Mackey used his
position as a lawyer to influence law enforcement is purely speculative and
does not raise a genuine issue for trial.

[
49
]

Mr. Jones states that he had worked with Mr.
Grosz between early December 2016 and January 2017 when Mr. Grosz was a paralegal
at GLC. At that time, Mr. Jones was providing legal services to Ms. Guo.
Mr. Grosz alleges that Mr. Jones, on or about August 1, 2017, filed a
false statement with the Richmond RCMP which caused him to be arrested and held
for 13 days under the
Mental Health Act,
R.S.B.C. 1996, c. 288. Mr.
Jones states that he was not in contact with the RCMP concerning Mr. Grosz prior
to his detention in August 2017. Mr. Jones does explain what contact he did
have with the RCMP, and he states:

13.  In late
August 2017 Mr. Grosz contacted me and a number of other people threatening a
lawsuit against Ms. Guo. Initially his claim was for a few thousand dollars for
alleged unpaid wages and overtime. Given that he and I had, until that point,
enjoyed a good relationship, I attempted to discuss the possibility of
settlement with Mr. Grosz. However by the time I contacted him his demands had
changed. Mr. Grosz said that if Ms. Guo did not settle with him he would send
to the RCMP, the Law Society and others allegations of impropriety against Ms.
Guo. In particular, he threatened to distribute lurid and outrageous
allegations, including photographs of a sexual device he implied was somehow
connected with Ms. Guo. I forwarded this information to Cst. Wu of the Richmond
RCMP, who I understood to be investigating complaints of harassment and
extortion made by Ms. Guo arising from earlier incidents. Attached as
Exhibit
E
to this my Affidavit is the email I sent to Cst Wu, which was later also
forwarded to Cst. Bevan.

[
50
]

I am satisfied that Mr. Jones has met the onus
of showing that there is no genuine issue with respect to the claim that he
filed a false statement to the RCMP in August 2017.

[
51
]

Mr. Grosz further asserts that Mr. Jones was in
the gallery on November 1, 2017, the date the defendants’ application to set
aside the default judgment in the First Guo Action was scheduled. Mr. Jones
states that on November 1, 2017 he was not in Vancouver that day. He was in
Kamloops where he was working as a professor. On that day, he taught his course
and went for lunch on campus. I accept this evidence.

[
52
]

Mr. Grosz has provided no evidence to support
either of the assertions made. In any event, attending court is not in itself
actionable conduct, and Mr. Grosz has provided no pleadings or evidence to
support his belief that Mr. Jones’ alleged attendance in court involved conduct
that was actionable.

[
53
]

The final allegation against Mr. Jones is that
he attached to an affidavit in the First Guo Action a confidential document,
being a medical report, which was in breach of “solicitor-client privilege”.
Mr. Jones explains the circumstances of his receipt of the medical report in
his affidavit. He states that on July 9, 2017, he received an email from Mr.
Grosz that “appeared plainly delusional”. A copy of the email is attached to
the affidavit. He replied to Mr. Grosz on July 10, 2017, expressing concern for
his mental wellbeing and asking that he pursue treatment. Mr. Grosz responded
to him the same day attaching a report from a psychiatrist. I do not see the
need to set out the particulars of the report, but it provides a medical
diagnosis for Mr. Grosz.

[
54
]

It is clear to me that the medical report was not
provided by Mr. Grosz to Mr. Jones in the context of a solicitor-client
relationship. Accordingly, I am satisfied that there is no genuine issue for
trial and the claims against any of the Lawyer defendants and Mr. Mackey must
be dismissed under R. 9-6(5)(a). I will go on to address the arguments raised
by these defendants under R. 9-5(1) as well.

Issue 2: Should the pleadings be
struck and the proceeding dismissed pursuant to R. 9-5(1)(a), (b) and (d)?

Legal Principles

[
55
]

Each of the defendants in this action apply to
have the pleadings struck and the action dismissed pursuant to R. 9-5(1), which
provides:

At any stage of a proceeding, the court may
order to be struck out or amended the whole or any part of a pleading, petition
or other document on the ground that

(a)

it discloses no reasonable claim or defence, as the case may be,

(b)

it is unnecessary, scandalous, frivolous or vexatious,

(c)

it may prejudice, embarrass or delay the fair trial or hearing of
the proceeding, or

(d)

it is otherwise an abuse of the process of the court,

and the court
may pronounce judgment or order the proceeding to be stayed or dismissed and
may order the costs of the application to be paid as special costs.

[
56
]

Each of the defendants relies on R. 9-5(1)(a),
(b), and (d).

[
57
]

I will reproduce my comments under this heading
from my reasons in
Grosz v. Royal Trust
,
2020 BCSC 128
at paras.
58–65

(the “Second Royal Trust Reasons”), as the law in this area has not changed:

On a motion to strike for not disclosing a
reasonable cause of action under R. 9-5(1)(a), the applicable test is whether
it is plain and obvious, assuming the facts pleaded to be true, that the
pleading discloses no reasonable cause of action:
R. v. Imperial Tobacco
Canada Ltd.
,
2011 SCC 42
at para.
17
. However, where the facts pleaded
are based purely on assumptions or wild speculations or are incapable of proof,
they may be subject to scrutiny by the court, albeit with great caution:
Young
v. Borzoni et al
,
2007 BCCA 16
at paras.
25–31
;
McDaniel v.
McDaniel,
2009 BCCA 53
at para.
22
.

The purpose of R. 9-5(1)(a) is to ensure the
parties and the court have a clear understanding of the nature of the claims
advanced. A party pleading a particular claim must plead assertions of fact
which would establish the essential elements of a successful claim if proven.
Prolix, convoluted, and incomprehensible pleadings do not lend themselves to
permit the parties to have a clear understanding of the claims advanced:
Gill
v. Canada
,
2013 BCSC 1703
at para.
7
.

The Court is not required to assume as true wide-sweeping,
inflammatory allegations of criminal conduct against the defendants. The court
is entitled to subject them to “skeptical analysis” and not to assume they are
true:
Stephen v. HMTQ,
2008 BCSC 1656
at para.
60
.

The case of
Ontario Consumers Home
Services Inc. v. Enercare Inc
.,
2014 ONSC 4154
at paras.
24-29
[
Ontario
Consumers
] provides a helpful summary of the applicable principles when a
pleading of conspiracy is made. Such a pleading requires the facts to be stated
with a heightened precision and clarity, being that conspiracy is an
intentional tort and a serious allegation. It is insufficient to lump all of
the defendants together into a general allegation of conspiracy, and bald or
speculative conclusions are not sufficient to support a claim and must be
struck.

In
Willow v. Chong
,
2013 BCSC 1083
at
para.
20
, Justice Fisher, as she then was, summarized the test for
striking a pleading under R. 9-5(1)(b):

Under Rule
9-5(1)(b), a pleading is unnecessary or vexatious if it does not go to
establishing the plaintiff’s cause of action, if it does not advance any claim
known in law, where it is obvious that an action cannot succeed, or where it
would serve no useful purpose and would be a waste of the court’s time and
public resources:
Citizens for Foreign Aid Reform Inc. v Canadian Jewish
Congress
,
1999 CanLII 5860 (BC SC)
, [1999] B.C.J. No. 2160 (S.C.);
Skender v Farley
,
2007
BCCA 629
. If a pleading is so confusing that it is difficult to understand what
is pleaded, it may also be unnecessary, frivolous or vexatious. An application
under this sub-rule may be supported by evidence.

In
Re Lang Michener and Fabian
(1987),

1987 CanLII 172 (ON SC)
, 37 D.L.R. (4th) 685 (Ont. H.C.J.) at 691, the court outlined the following
non-exhaustive list of principles to consider when determining whether an
action is vexatious, which has been repeatedly endorsed by the B.C. Courts (see
for example:
Simon v. Canada (Attorney General)
,
2015 BCSC 924
at para.
97
,
aff’d
2016 BCCA 52
[
Simon
]):

(a)

the bringing of one or more actions to determine an issue which has
already been determined by a court of competent jurisdiction constitutes a
vexatious proceeding;

(b)

where it is obvious that an action cannot succeed, or if the action
would lead to no possible good, or if no reasonable person can reasonably
expect to obtain relief, the action is vexatious;

(c)

vexatious actions include those brought for an improper purpose,
including the harassment and oppression of other parties by multifarious
proceedings brought for purposes other than the assertion of legitimate rights;

(d)

it is a general characteristic of vexatious proceedings that grounds
and issues raised tend to be rolled forward into subsequent actions and
repeated and supplemented, often with actions brought against the lawyers who
have acted for or against the litigant in earlier proceedings;

(e)

in determining whether proceedings are vexatious, the court must
look at the whole history of the matter and not just whether there was
originally a good cause of action;

(f)

the failure of the person instituting the proceedings to pay the
costs of unsuccessful proceedings is one factor to be considered in determining
whether proceedings are vexatious; and

(g)

the respondent’s conduct in persistently taking unsuccessful appeals
form judicial decisions can be considered vexatious conduct of legal
proceedings.

…

The doctrine of
abuse of process allows the court to prevent a claim from proceeding where to
do so would violate principles of judicial economy, consistency, finality, and
integrity of the administration of justice:
Toronto (City) v. C.U.P.E.,
Local 79
,
2003 SCC 63
at para.
37
. When determining whether the
proceedings constitute an abuse of process, the court may consider whether its
process is being used dishonestly or unfairly, or for some ulterior or improper
purpose, and whether there have been multiple or successive related proceedings
that are likely to cause vexation or oppression:
Young
at paras.
65–66
.
Bringing a series of successive related proceedings is an abuse of the court’s
process, even where the plaintiff sincerely believes that earlier decisions
were wrong and that he has not been treated fairly:
Budgell v. Oppal
,

2007 BCSC 991
at para.
28
, aff’d
2008 BCCA 349
.

Position of the Defendants

Rule 9-5(1)(a): Do the pleadings
fail to disclose a reasonable claim against the defendants?

[
58
]

The defendants all argue that the pleadings
disclose no reasonable claim against them and the allegations of conspiracy and
fraud are based on assumptions and unprovable wild speculation without
foundation. They all argue that Mr. Grosz has failed to plead facts that

the arguments made by some of the defendants respecting specific issues raised
against them.

[
59
]

Mr. Munro submits that the notice of civil claim
fails to plead any material facts that support the elements of any of the
causes of actions against him.

[
60
]

He further argues that Mr. Grosz never sought
nor obtained leave of the Court to commence this action against him, and as a
result of the operation of
s. 215
of the
BIA
,

this proceedings is
a nullity. Section 215 of the
BIA
states:

Except by leave
of the court, no action lies against the Superintendent, an official receiver,
an interim receiver or a trustee with respect to any report made under, or any
action taken pursuant to, this Act.

[
61
]

Mr. Munro submits that this requirement for
leave to commence an action against a trustee is designed to protect the
trustee against frivolous or vexatious actions or actions which have no basis
in fact and which would otherwise interfere with the due administration of the
insolvent estate by the trustee so that the purposes of the
BIA
will not
be frustrated:
GMAC Commercial Credit Corporation - Canada v. T.C.T.
Logistics Inc.,
2006 SCC 35
at paras.
55 and 58
[
GMAC
];
Braich

(Re),
2007 BCSC 1604
at para.
13
.

[
62
]

The Lawyer defendants submit that the
allegations on their face disclose no cause of action known to law. They argue
that counsel owes no duty to an adverse party and allegations that the opposing
party has misled or intentionally deceived the court resulting in decisions or
rulings unfavourable to him do not find actionable breaches of any private duty
owed to him:
Pearlman v. Critchley
,
2012 BCSC 1830
at para.
44
;
Singh
v. Nielsen
,
2016 BCSC 2420
at para.
20
.

[
63
]

They further argue that any allegedly defamatory
communications made by them in the course of or incidental to the litigation in
the First Guo Action on behalf of their clients are protected by absolute
privilege:
Hamouth v. Edwards & Angell
,
2005 BCCA 172
at paras.
2–3
,
21–22, 29–40;
Lawrence v. Sandilands
,
2003 BCSC 211
at paras.
90–93
.

[
64
]

Finally, they argue that the principle of
witness immunity prevents claims against prospective witnesses in respect of
their evidence whether in civil conspiracy, negligence, breach of
confidentiality, or some other form:
Workum v. Olnick et al.
,
2005 BCSC
1262
at paras.
7
, 19, dismissed without affirming
2006 BCCA 528
;
Hung v.
Gardiner
,
2003 BCCA 257
at paras.
33–37
.

Rule 9-5(1)(b) and (d): are the
pleadings unnecessary, frivolous, vexatious or an abuse of process?

[
65
]

The defendants argue that the notice of civil
claim does not plead allegations that support any of the causes of action
pleaded, provides no substance, and is designed to harass the defendants and
put them through unnecessary trouble and expense.

[
66
]

The Lawyer defendants submit that this
proceeding was brought for an improper purpose as an attempt by Mr. Grosz to
disqualify or otherwise deprive opposing parties to the litigation of counsel,
which is an abuse of process.

[
67
]

The defendants argue that this action was
commenced in bad faith. It is another attempt by Mr. Grosz to advance his
“animus” against Ms. Guo and all persons who Mr. Grosz perceives as being
connected to Ms. Guo, including her former counsel. It is further an attempt to
re-litigate and circumvent the release and CDO in the First Guo Action. They
point out that this action is one of multiple successive proceedings commenced
by Mr. Grosz and the indiscriminate allegations in the notice of civil claim
are clearly vexatious and oppressive.

Analysis

[
68
]

I will consider all of the arguments made under
Rule 9-5(1)(a), (b) and (d) since, while they address different concerns, there
is significant overlap between them.

[
69
]

I am satisfied that it is plain and obvious that
the claims against the defendants offend R. 9-5(1)(a), (b) and (d). It is clear
that this action is vexatious, frivolous, and an abuse of process.

[
70
]

The claim against Mr. Munro cannot be brought
without leave, and no leave was granted. More fundamentally, there are no facts
pled that support any claim against Mr. Munro. There is an allegation made that
Mr. Munro took the position that Mr. Grosz was not a creditor of GLC since he
had consented to the dismissal of the First Guo Action. Mr. Grosz has failed to
explain why that position was in any way improper or incorrect, or why any
claim against Mr. Munro should arise as a result.

[
71
]

It is clear to me that Mr. Grosz commenced this
action to try to have counsel for the Guo defendants and FTI disqualified from
acting.

[
72
]

In the notice of civil claim, Mr. Grosz does not
advance any particulars of a claim against Mr. Brousson except to allege that
some conspiracy existed. It is not clear to me what the allegations are against
Mr. Louman-Gardiner except that he acted for the Guo defendants and also
participated in some type of conspiracy, no particulars of which were provided.

[
73
]

The allegation against Mr. McLean is that he
informed a master in chambers that his law partner was counsel for the Proposal
Trustee. Mr. Grosz claims that this was a “false submission”, but provided no
details on why this was false or, even if it was, what basis Mr. Grosz had to
sue him because of it.

[
74
]

There is an allegation against Mr. Jones that he
attached to an affidavit a medical report that Mr. Grosz says was confidential
and was received by Mr. Jones in the context of a solicitor-client
relationship. The notice of civil claim alleges that Mr. Jones agreed to act
for Mr. Grosz
pro bono
in December 2016 to approach the Credential
Committee of the Law Society of British Columbia to make them aware of certain
facts that Mr. Grosz would have to report. I have not assumed these allegations
to be true since, in my view, this is the type of case that requires a
“skeptical analysis” to be applied. Mr. Jones denies that he was ever retained
by or that he ever provided legal advice to Mr. Grosz. He advises that he
received the medical report in July 2017 when Mr. Grosz was sending him emails
that raised a grave concern in Mr. Jones’ mind over Mr. Grosz’s mental health.
At this time, Mr. Grosz was still employed at GLC. As I explained earlier
in these reasons, there is also no basis for a claim against Mr. Jones with
respect to his alleged attendance in chambers on November 1, 2017, or with
respect to him filing a complaint with the RCMP. I find that the allegations
against him in the notice of civil claim are frivolous and vexatious and
brought as an attempt to harass or inconvenience lawyers who have acted for Ms.
Guo.

[
75
]

With respect to the Guo defendants, I find that
Mr. Grosz is attempting to circumvent the CDO that he agreed to, dismissing the
First Guo Action. He is essentially attempting to rely on the same factual
matrix as against her, as evidenced by his attaching the notice of civil claim
in the First Guo Action as a Schedule. This is vexatious and an abuse of
process.

[
76
]

Many of the allegations advanced in this action
surround the circumstances of Mr. Grosz agreeing to a settlement in the First
Guo Action and his view that he was the subject of an “extortion”. I heard the
application to set aside the CDO and I found there was no support for any of
Mr. Grosz’s allegations; see my CDO Reasons at paras. 106–128.

[
77
]

Mr. Grosz makes highly inflammatory allegations
of fraud, conspiracy, extortion, and criminal conduct against all of the
defendants, without sufficiently particularizing the claims or providing any
factual basis for such serious allegations. The claims are based on pure
speculation. It is not sufficient to make a general allegation of conspiracy,
and bald or speculative conclusions are not sufficient to support such a claim.

[
78
]

Mr. Grosz seems intent on suing or disqualifying
every lawyer that acts for any opposing party. I note that he provided notice to
the current counsel for the Lawyer defendants that he would seek to disqualify
him from acting in this and other actions. It appeared to me that the purpose
of this notice was to attempt to derail the hearing of the application
scheduled on December 3 and 4, 2019 in the Second Royal Trust Action, in which
Mr. Arvisais was acting for the Boughton defendants. I directed that no such
application would be permitted prior to the hearing of the application to
strike.

[
79
]

I reiterate my view stated in my reasons in the
Second Royal Trust Reasons at paras.
105 and 106
:

[105]    I am persuaded that Mr. Grosz
is using the court process in an abusive manner. He continues to use the threat
of a lawsuit as a means to achieve his personal goals, including to attempt to
extract settlements from the applicant defendants in circumstances where it is
obvious that the action cannot succeed and no reasonable person could expect a
court to grant relief.

[106]    I am
concerned by the use of judicial resources to fuel Mr. Grosz’s speculative
theories at an inordinate cost to the applicant defendants and to the detriment
of other litigants awaiting hearings. To allow the Second Action to continue
would be to allow the court’s process to be misused and to allow an oppressive
and vexatious action to continue against the applicant defendants.

[
80
]

My concerns are amplified by the actions Mr.
Grosz has taken in suing six lawyers and the Proposal Trustee. I see little
likelihood that Mr. Grosz will cease his oppressive and vexatious behavior.

[
81
]

Although Mr. Grosz provided no submissions, I
will operate on the basis that one of his arguments would have been that he
should have an opportunity to amend his pleadings. I have considered the nature
of the pleadings, my knowledge as the case management judge on a number of actions
Mr. Grosz has brought, and the extensive materials that I have been provided, and
have concluded that it would not be fair in the circumstances to allow him an
opportunity to amend.

[
82
]

In respect to Mr. Munro, Mr. Grosz needed to
seek leave to sue him. Although the threshold for leave is quite low, it should
not be granted where the claim is frivolous, vexatious, and does not disclose a
cause of action against a trustee:
GMAC
at para.
57
;
Re Braich
at
para. 21. This aptly describes the action against Mr. Munro, as well as
the other defendants.

[
83
]

Given the serious deficiencies in the pleadings,
the vexatious nature of the allegations, and the improper purposes for which
they were brought, it would not be appropriate to allow an amendment. In my
view, the appropriate remedy is to strike the pleadings and dismiss the action
against all of the defendants.

Issue 3: Should Mr. Grosz be
declared a vexatious litigant?

Legal Principles

[
84
]

Section 18
of the
Supreme Court Act

empowers
the Court to prohibit a person from instituting legal proceedings without prior
leave of the Court:

18
If, on application by any person, the court is satisfied that a
person has habitually, persistently and without reasonable grounds, instituted
vexatious legal proceedings in the Supreme Court or in the Provincial Court
against the same or different persons, the court may, after hearing that person
or giving him or her an opportunity to be heard
,
order that a legal proceeding must not, without leave of the court, be
instituted by that person in any court.

[
85
]

Section 18 confers a broad jurisdiction on the
court to control is own processes. This is a power that must not be used
lightly. The court must balance the important values underlying open court
access against the need to prevent the abuse of that right:
Semenoff Estate
v. Semenoff
,

2017 BCCA 17
at para.
31
, citing
S.(M.) v. S.(P.I.)
(1998),

1998 CanLII 15034 (BC CA)
, 60 B.C.L.R. (3d) 232 (C.A.), leave to appeal ref’d [1999] S.C.C.A. No. 11.

[
86
]

The court may consider proceedings before
administrative tribunals in determining whether an order under s. 18 is
appropriate:
Bajwa v. British Columbia Veterinary Medical Association.,
2012
BCSC 878
at para.
211
.

[
87
]

As helpfully summarized by Justice Iyer in
Rafique
v. AWM-Alliance Real Estate Group Ltd
.,
2019 BCSC 247
at para.
51
, citing
Carten
v. Carten
,
2015 BCCA 201
, key indicators of a vexatious proceeding include:

a)

bringing one or more actions to determine an issue which has already
been determined by a court of competent jurisdiction;

b)

it is obvious that the action cannot succeed, would lead to no
possible good, or no reasonable person can reasonably expect to obtain relief;

c)

the action is brought for an improper purpose, including the
harassment and oppression of other parties by multifarious proceedings brought
for purposes other than the assertion of legitimate rights;

d)

the grounds and issues in the first proceeding have been rolled
forward into subsequent actions and repeated and supplemented, often with
actions brought against the lawyers who have acted for or against the litigant
in earlier proceedings;

e)

the person who instituted the proceedings has failed to pay the
costs of the unsuccessful proceedings; and

f)

the person has persistently taken unsuccessful
appeals.

[
88
]

The ultimate question is whether the litigant
has taken himself over the line:
Lindsay v. Canada (Attorney General)
,

2005 BCCA 594
at para.
26
.

Position of the defendants

[
89
]

The Lawyer defendants submit that Mr. Grosz’s
conduct fits squarely within each of the key indicators of a vexatious litigant,
except in regard to persistently pursuing unsuccessful appeals.

[
90
]

They further submit that where a litigant has a
large number of vexatious proceedings already underway, those proceedings may
be stayed and leave required for any further steps, citing
Parchment v.
British Columbia
,
2015 BCSC 1006
at paras.
29–37
.

[
91
]

In support of the legal representation
requirement, the Lawyer defendants rely on the decision of
Unrau v. National
Dental Examining Board
,
2019 ABQB 283
at paras.
817–19
, which sets out the
types of factors that may be used to predict when an abusive litigant may
extend their litigation misconduct to the court’s leave process.

[
92
]

Finally, these defendants argue that the court
has authority to require leave before instituting or continuing proceedings
before a tribunal or other non-judicial decision maker when the litigant is an
abusive litigant:
Unrau

at paras.
853–63
.

[
93
]

Mr. Munro provided supplemental written
submissions on the impact of the Alberta Court of Appeal decision in
Jonsson
.
He relies on the following observations in that decision:

a.

Being “ill-informed or emotionally overwhelmed” does not excuse
vexatious behaviour [at para. 8];

b.

Vexatious litigant orders should only be used when other procedural
techniques are ineffective [at para. 12];

c.

Other procedural techniques listed by the Court include procedural
orders, case management orders, and sanctions for failure to comply;

d.

Citing
Trial Lawyers Association of British Columbia v British Columbia
(Attorney General),
2014 SCC 59

at para.
47
:  “There is no
constitutional right to bring frivolous or vexatious cases, and measures that
deter such cases may actually increase efficiency and overall access to
justice”;

e.

Resorting to any residual inherent jurisdiction to control vexatious
litigation should only be made when the provisions of the statute [in that
case, the
Judicature Act
] are inadequate to answer the problem and there
are compelling reasons to step beyond what the statute provides for [at para.
33];

f.

When conduct such as “hopeless proceedings”,
“collateral attacks”, “making unsubstantiated allegations of misconduct”, and
“initiating ‘busybody’ lawsuits” is persistent, vexatious litigant orders may
be justified. Individual occurrences should be dealt with via specific remedies
such as striking pleadings or summary dismissal [at para. 40]; and

g.

The response to problematic litigation must find the proper balance
between maintaining reasonable access to the court, while preserving court
resources and shielding other litigants from abusive behavior [at para. 16].

[
94
]

This defendant argues that a distinguishing
factor of the
Jonsson

decision was that Mr. Jonsson was not the party
commencing or continuing proceedings but defending them, albeit in an inappropriate
manner. Mr. Grosz has been the instigator of proceedings. In addition,
procedural techniques such as case-management orders and cost sanctions have
done little to curb Mr. Grosz’s abusive behaviors.

Analysis

[
95
]

When I apply the legal principles to the
circumstances of this case, it is clear to me that the application should be
granted. I agree with the defendants’ submission that practically all of the
key indicators of vexatious proceedings are present.

[
96
]

Mr. Grosz has consistently sought to bring actions
or applications to determine issues that have already been decided, or to roll
the grounds and issues in prior proceedings forward into subsequent actions
with actions brought against the lawyers who have acted for the opposing
parties. This is precisely what occurred in both this action and in the Royal
Trust action. In both cases, Mr. Grosz expressly repleaded the allegations made
in the first notices of civil claim in the second notices of civil claim, and
attached the earlier notices of civil claim as schedules to the second ones. He
repeated and supplemented the allegations, and also sued the lawyers acting for
the other side, being the Boughton defendants in the Royal Trust action and the
Lawyer defendants in this action.

[
97
]

Mr. Grosz has been clear that his purpose in
suing the various lawyers he has sued is to have them disqualified or to punish
them for acting for their clients. In order to achieve these goals, he has made
very serious allegations of professional misconduct and conspiracy against
these lawyers, without having any support for such allegations other than
speculation. He has made these allegations in court, including in pleadings,
submissions and affidavits, as well as to the police, the Law Society, and
various third parties. His correspondence uses very offensive and demeaning
language in describing these lawyers. Mr. Grosz’s status as a self-represented
litigant and any frustration he may have with the court process does not excuse
him from this behaviour.

[
98
]

Mr. Grosz has threatened to apply to disqualify
lawyers, to sue them, and to have them disciplined by the Law Society if they
continue to act for their clients, and he has followed through on those
threats. He has also threatened to bring further and more serious actions
against opposing parties if they do not agree to settle his claims.

[
99
]

Mr. Grosz has also incorporated a society
through which he brought another action, the Minoru Action, against the Guo
defendants and over 20 other defendants. As there is a pending application to
strike in that proceeding, I wish to be clear that I make no comment on the
merits of that case. I raise it only to note that if one includes the action
Mr. Grosz is attempting to start in the Federal Court against the Guo defendants
and various other parties referenced earlier in these reasons, this is the
fourth action that Mr. Grosz has brought against the Guo defendants. This does
not include the two private informations of four counts each that Mr. Grosz
swore against Ms. Guo in Provincial Court, or Mr. Grosz’s application to add
himself as a party or to be appointed the receiver in bankruptcy in the
Insolvency Proceeding.

[
100
]

This decision is one of several in which I have found that Mr. Grosz
brought the action or application for an improper purpose or for which no
reasonable person could expect to obtain relief (see the Second Royal Trust
Reasons at paras.
99 and 105
, and the CDO Reasons at para. 123). I do not make
this observation lightly, but it is fair to say that Mr. Grosz has used the
process of the court and other tribunals and administrative bodies for the
purpose of harassing these defendants and others.

[
101
]

To give some context to the scope of Mr. Grosz’s activity, I note
that, on the defendants’ count, Mr. Grosz is a party to approximately 17
proceedings, and has sought to add himself as a party or
amicus curiae

in 19 other Supreme Court proceedings. He has brought or threatened to bring
actions or complaints against many different lawyers and law firms, the university
that Mr. Jones teaches at, the Law Society of BC, the Lawyers’ Insurance Fund,
certain benchers, certain individuals who were involved in the Insolvency
Proceeding, the Richmond RCMP, Crown counsel, the Access Pro Bono Society of
BC, the Director of Civil Forfeiture, the Superintendent of Bankruptcy, the
director of CSIS, and the commissioner of the RCMP. He has also accused several
judges of this Court of conspiring against him. In addition to his use of court
proceedings at this Court, the Provincial Court, and the Federal Court, he has
brought or threatened to bring about consequences to various individuals
through complaining to the RCMP, the Vancouver Police, the Ministry of Citizen
Services, the Law Society of BC, the Office of the Superintendent of
Bankruptcy, the Information and Privacy Commissioner for BC, and the Human
Rights Tribunal.

[
102
]

Mr. Grosz’s actions have also impacted the court staff, including
registry staff and judicial administrative assistants. I outlined some of my
concerns in this regard in my memoranda of November 8 and 15, 2019, in which I
explained to Mr. Grosz that it is inappropriate to attempt to communicate with
me about cases before me without counsel present, to file notices to act in
person or to make applications in actions in which he is not a party, to send
emails or letters to the court registry staff or legal counsel asking them to
forward the communications or unfiled materials to a judge, or to overwhelm the
court registry staff with phone calls and voicemail messages. I ordered that
Mr. Grosz is only to communicate with court registry staff using the formal
processes outlined in the applicable practice directions and that he is
required to comply with the case management orders I made with respect to the
filing of affidavits and bringing of applications in the manners of which I was
seized.

[
103
]

Despite my instructions and orders, Mr. Grosz continued to email the
court registry, the Court’s legal counsel, the Chief Justice, and myself,
frequently attaching voluminous materials and copying numerous third parties,
sometimes without copying counsel or parties in the litigation. He also has
issued “News Releases” about his cases to a large number of recipients, some of
which have included confidential information and information covered by
solicitor-client privilege (see my Injunction Reasons beginning at para. 35).
While I am mindful of the fact that Mr. Grosz is self-represented, he has legal
training and experience working as a paralegal and he has been informed on
numerous occasions by myself, other judges, and legal counsel about the
appropriate procedures to follow and why they are necessary. He has chosen to
ignore these instructions.

[
104
]

Although Mr. Grosz has not persistently taken unsuccessful appeals,
he has indicated that he intends to seek review of every order I make in the
Court of Appeal. He appears to have taken the same approach with orders made by
other judges.

[
105
]

I am satisfied that Mr. Grosz must be declared a vexatious litigant
as other procedural techniques have been ineffective in incentivizing him to
restrain his conduct. In my capacity as case management judge in various
actions involving Mr. Grosz since August 2019, he has consistently
disregarded the court’s directions and orders. He has produced thousands of
pages of materials in actions started for improper purposes, forcing the
defendants to devote significant amounts of time and resources to respond to
meritless claims. He has sent in numerous requests to appear, often seeking the
same relief that has already been denied.

[
106
]

While I understand that he is frustrated and overwhelmed by the
number of actions he is participating in, it is not fair to take this
frustration out on opposing parties or court staff, nor is it a reason to
disregard court orders or the
Rules
. There is no doubt the importance of
all individuals having access to the court, but in balancing that principle
against the need to prevent the abuse of that right, in the circumstances of
this case, I am satisfied that an order under
s. 18
of the
Supreme Court Act

is warranted. I am satisfied that Mr. Grosz has habitually, persistently, and
without reasonable grounds, instituted vexatious legal proceedings in this
Court against the Guo defendants and various other parties.

Issue 4: What terms should be
imposed on any vexatious order granted?

Legal Principles

[
107
]

There is case authority in this province that supports that a
litigant may be restricted to only filing documents or proceedings by a
solicitor acting on their behalf:  see
Household Trust Co. v. Golden Horse
Farms Inc
.,
1992 CanLII 420
(B.C.C.A.); see also
Unrau

at paras.

817–819
.

[
108
]

In the
Jonsson
case, the Court notes that vexatious litigant
orders are “tolerable because they do not foreclose all access to the court,
and merely perform a gatekeeping function. Insurmountable preconditions,
however, effectively amount to a total barrier to court access”: at para. 67.

[
109
]

The Alberta Court of Appeal further noted that most self-represented
litigants are unrepresented because they cannot afford a lawyer. Requiring a
vexatious litigant to obtain a lawyer presents a financial barrier that may be
insurmountable: at para. 71.

Position of the Defendants

[
110
]

In addition to the order that Mr. Grosz not initiate any new
proceedings without leave of the Court, the Lawyer defendants sought the
following additional terms:

a)

That the First Guo Action and the Minoru Action be stayed and that
Mr. Grosz may not take any further steps in them without first obtaining leave
of the Court, and that those actions will be dismissed if leave is not sought
within two weeks of the order and, if leave is sought, if leave is not obtained
within three months of the order;

b)

Mr. Grosz may not initiate or continue any involvement in any
existing proceeding in which he is not a party without first obtaining leave of
the Court;

c)

Subject to any statutory provision restricting the scope of the
order, Mr. Grosz may not initiate any proceeding before any statutory tribunal
or other official adjudicative body without first obtaining leave of the Court;
and

d)

That Mr. Grosz may not seek leave on any matter except either (a)
through counsel authorized to practice law in the Province of British Columbia
or (b) upon paying security for costs of the leave application.

[
111
]

The Guo defendants and Mr. Munro, in their
application response, sought a further term to the vexatious litigant order,
being:

Robert W.G.
Grosz should not hereafter, without leave of this Court, file any documents or
proceedings except by a member of the Law Society of British Columbia in good
standing acting on his behalf.

[
112
]

These defendants, in oral submissions, submitted that this term
would require Mr. Grosz to file any documents in ongoing proceedings through a
lawyer, and to file any new proceedings for which leave has been granted
through a lawyer, unless Mr. Grosz obtained leave of the court to act on his
own behalf. Mr. Grosz would not be required to engage a lawyer in order to
obtain leave to act on his own behalf.

[
113
]

In the Supplemental Submissions of Mr. Munro,
his position was that the order should at least contain the following terms:

a.

Robert W.G. Grosz, either directly or indirectly, on his own behalf
or on behalf of another, shall not hereafter without leave of this Court:

i.

Commence any legal proceedings in any court;

ii.

Initiate or continue any involvement, including
the filing of documents or pleadings, in any existing proceeding in which he is
not a party.

Analysis

[
114
]

With respect to the stays in the First Guo Action and the Minoru
Action, it is my view that the order should not be granted. The status of the
First Guo Action is that it is dismissed. The application to set aside the CDO
has been dismissed. The only further step Mr. Grosz could take is to appeal the
dismissal decision. This will be a matter for the Court of Appeal. With respect
to the Minoru Action, it is now being case managed by a different judge. There
are pending applications by the majority of the defendants in that action to
have the action dismissed. I am of the view that this is a matter for the case
management judge in the Minoru Action to deal with and I will not make any
orders in respect to that action.

[
115
]

Mr. Grosz has threatened to add himself as a party or
amicus
curiae
in approximately 19 other actions. It is not clear to me on what
possible basis Mr. Grosz would have the right to add himself as a party. I
agree that if Mr. Grosz seeks to bring an application in any action in which he
is not a party, he must seek leave to do so.

[
116
]

My view is that it is not appropriate to order a condition that Mr.
Grosz have authorized counsel act for him on the leave application, nor in any
current or future actions, since it would effectively deny Mr. Grosz’s access
to justice. I agree with the Alberta Court of Appeal’s description that such
requirements would create an “insurmountable barrier” for Mr. Grosz, who has
consistently been granted indigent status. It is important to recognize that
Mr. Grosz is not being denied his right to bring a claim; only to have a
justice perform a gatekeeping role so that vexatious and frivolous actions and
applications are not pursued.

[
117
]

Although it appears that Mr. Grosz may have commenced vexatious
matters in various statutory tribunals, I am not convinced that I should be
making an order barring him from commencing proceedings in any court or other
adjudicative body. At this stage, I am of the view that the order should be
restricted to the BC Supreme Court.

[
118
]

Mr. Grosz’s activity in Provincial Court is limited to swearing two
private criminal informations against Ms. Guo. Absent express language, an
order restricting his right to commence proceedings in any court would not
apply to a matter such as filing a private information under the provisions of
the
Criminal Code
:
Attorney General of B.C. v.

Lindsay
,

2007 BCCA 165

at para.
29
. In any event, it is unclear whether this
court has jurisdiction under
s. 18
of the
Supreme Court Act
to make such
an order:
Parchment
at paras.
38–49
. I am not convinced that the extent
of Mr. Grosz’s activity in Provincial Court is such that he should be
required to obtain leave before commencing proceedings in that court at this
time.

[
119
]

I am also of the view that requiring Mr. Grosz to post security for
costs of the leave applications is not appropriate. An individual who is
declared a vexatious litigant is required to follow Administrative Notice 16.

The
potential defendants to the proposed actions are not given notice of the leave
application. The time is spent by judges or masters who are assigned to review
the leave applications. In such circumstances, it is not appropriate to require
Mr. Grosz to post any security.

Conclusion

[
120
]

I conclude that Mr. Grosz’s claim against the Lawyer defendants and
Mr. Mackey should be struck, pursuant to R. 9-6, as raising no genuine
issue for trial.

[
121
]

I also conclude that the pleadings offend R. 9-5(1)(a), (b) and (d)
as disclosing no reasonable cause of action and being vexatious, frivolous, and
an abuse of process. As such, the pleadings are struck and the proceeding
dismissed against all of the defendants.

[
122
]

Pursuant to
s. 18
of the
Supreme Court Act
, Mr. Grosz, in his
name, or as an officer or director of a company, or in the name of a society he
has incorporated, on his own behalf or on behalf of another, is prohibited from
directly or indirectly instituting any legal proceeding in this Court, without
prior leave of the Court.

[
123
]

Mr. Grosz must seek leave of the Court to file an application or
materials in any existing proceeding in which he is not a party.

[
124
]

In the notices of application, the defendants have sought special
costs, in some cases payable on a lump sum basis. The defendants are entitled
to special costs. Mr. Grosz’s conduct has been reprehensible on many levels.
His actions have clearly been abusive towards the court system, the litigants,
and their counsel. He continuously makes, without foundation, serious
accusations of fraud, conspiracy, and criminal conduct against many of the
parties. He has maintained proceedings which are vexatious and without any
reasonable grounds.  His actions are deserving of rebuke.

[
125
]

I am not prepared to order lump sum special costs for the same
reasons set out in my costs reasons in the Second Royal Trust Action, indexed
at
2020 BCSC 1083
. I am not satisfied that I have a sufficient evidentiary
basis to make such an order.

[
126
]

The signature of Mr. Grosz on the form of the
order is dispensed with.

“Forth J.”
